stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What forms at each electrode?

options.content: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: Hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode and hydroxide ions at the anode.

options.content: oxygen at the cathode and hydrogen at the anode
options.rationale: This is reversed: hydrogen ions are positive, so they go to the cathode.

options.content: hydrogen at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
options.rationale: Sulfate ions are not discharged.

options.content: sulfur at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: No sulfur is formed; the acid is not decomposed.

explanation: The acid provides ions so that the water conducts. Hydrogen forms at the cathode and oxygen at the anode: in effect, water is decomposed.

stem: True or false: when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes, sodium metal forms at the cathode.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: It is false. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: hydrogen forms at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen.

explanation: In aqueous solution, hydrogen ions (from the water) are discharged at the cathode instead of sodium ions, so hydrogen is produced. Sodium metal can be made only by electrolysing molten sodium chloride.

stem: Acidified water is electrolysed. What is the ratio of the volume of hydrogen to the volume of oxygen produced?

options.rationale: This is reversed: there is more hydrogen than oxygen.
This ratio applies to hydrogen and chlorine from brine, not to water.
Two hydrogen molecules form for every oxygen molecule: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂.
8 : 1 is roughly the ratio of the masses of oxygen to hydrogen, not the volumes of the gases.

explanation: The overall reaction is 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, so the volume of hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen.

stem: Name the gas produced at the **anode** when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes.

rejected.feedback: Oxygen forms from a dilute chloride solution; with a concentrated solution chlorine forms.
Chloride is the ion; the gas formed is chlorine.

explanation: Chloride ions are attracted to the anode, and because they are concentrated they are discharged: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. The pale yellow-green gas is chlorine.

stem: Which test confirms that the gas collected at the **cathode** during the electrolysis of dilute sulfuric acid is hydrogen?

options.content: It burns with a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.
options.rationale: Hydrogen burns rapidly in air with a pop.

options.content: It relights a glowing splint held inside the tube.
options.rationale: That is the test for oxygen, which forms at the anode.
That is the test for chlorine.
That is the test for carbon dioxide.

explanation: Hydrogen forms at the cathode. A lighted splint held at the mouth of the tube gives a squeaky pop as the hydrogen burns.

stem: Why is water acidified with a little dilute sulfuric acid before it is electrolysed?

options.content: The acid reacts with the platinum electrodes to make them conduct electricity.
options.rationale: The platinum or graphite electrodes already conduct, and they are inert.

options.content: Pure water contains very few ions, so it conducts electricity very poorly.
options.rationale: The acid adds ions, so a current can flow.

options.content: The acid is the source of the oxygen gas.
options.rationale: The oxygen comes from the water (its hydroxide ions); the acid is not used up.

options.content: The acid stops the hydrogen and oxygen from mixing.
options.rationale: The gases are kept apart by collecting them in separate tubes.

explanation: Water is only very slightly ionised, so pure water is a poor conductor. Adding sulfuric acid supplies plenty of ions. The acid is not used up: it becomes more concentrated as water is decomposed.

stem: After concentrated aqueous sodium chloride has been electrolysed for some time, what is left in the solution?

options.rationale: Both chlorine and hydrogen leave the solution as gases; the solution becomes alkaline, not acidic.
Sodium is not discharged from aqueous solution.
Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain after H₂ and Cl₂ are given off.
The sodium ions and hydroxide ions stay in solution.

explanation: Hydrogen ions are discharged at the cathode and chloride ions at the anode. The sodium ions and hydroxide ions are left, so the solution becomes sodium hydroxide, an alkali.
hints: Which two ions are NOT discharged?

stem: Acidified water is electrolysed in a Hofmann voltameter. After 15 minutes, 36 cm³ of hydrogen has been collected. Predict the volume of oxygen collected in the same time.
explanation: The volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2 : 1, so the volume of oxygen is half the volume of hydrogen: 36 ÷ 2 = 18 cm³.
hints: Which gas is produced in the larger volume?

stem:
A student electrolyses acidified water in a Hofmann voltameter and records the volume of gas in each tube.

| Time / min | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Volume of hydrogen / cm³ | 6.0 | 12.1 | 18.0 | 24.2 | 30.1 |
| Volume of oxygen / cm³ | 2.6 | 5.7 | 8.8 | 11.9 | 15.0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: At which electrode is the hydrogen collected?

options.rationale: Oxygen is collected at the anode.
Each gas forms at one electrode only.
Hydrogen ions are positive and are discharged at the negative cathode.
No gas forms in the reservoir; there is no electrode there.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the ratio volume of hydrogen ÷ volume of oxygen after 5 minutes. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how these results show that the formula of water is H₂O.

points.description: Equal volumes of gases (at the same temperature and pressure) contain equal numbers of molecules
So 2 molecules of H₂ form for every 1 molecule of O₂, giving 4 H atoms to 2 O atoms
Ratio of H : O atoms is 2 : 1, so the formula is H₂O

parts.explanation: The volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen is 2 : 1. Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, so two H₂ molecules form for every O₂ molecule. That is 4 hydrogen atoms for every 2 oxygen atoms, a ratio of 2 : 1, so water is H₂O.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: After 1 minute the volume of oxygen is a little less than half the volume of hydrogen. Suggest why.

points.description: Some oxygen dissolves in the water (oxygen is more soluble than hydrogen) until the water is saturated

parts.explanation: Oxygen is slightly more soluble in water than hydrogen, so at first some of the oxygen dissolves instead of being collected.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe the test that confirms the gas at the anode is oxygen.

accepted.value: a glowing splint bursts into flame

rejected.feedback: The squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen.
That is the test for hydrogen.

explanation: Hydrogen is collected at the cathode and oxygen at the anode. After 5 minutes 30.1 ÷ 15.0 = 2.0, so the volume ratio is 2 : 1. Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules, so the atom ratio H : O is 2 : 1 and the formula of water is H₂O. Early on, a little oxygen dissolves in the water.
workedSolution:
**(b)** $30.1 \div 15.0 = 2.007 \approx 2.0$.

**(c)** 2 molecules $\ce{H2}$ : 1 molecule $\ce{O2}$ → 4 H atoms : 2 O atoms → H : O = 2 : 1 → $\ce{H2O}$.
hints: Equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules.
Each hydrogen molecule has two atoms, and so does each oxygen molecule.

stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using **graphite** electrodes. What are the products?

options.content: copper at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so it is deposited; sulfate ions are not discharged, so oxygen forms.

options.content: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper (not hydrogen) forms at the cathode.

options.content: copper at the cathode and sulfur dioxide at the anode
options.rationale: Sulfate ions are not discharged.

options.content: copper at the cathode, while the anode dissolves
options.rationale: Graphite is inert, so it does not dissolve; that happens with a copper anode.

explanation:
Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (pink-brown deposit). Anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (bubbles). The blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Compare the reactivity of copper and hydrogen.

stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using **copper** electrodes. What happens to the blue colour of the solution?

options.rationale: It fades with inert electrodes, because then copper(II) ions are removed and not replaced.
Copper(II) ions enter the solution at the anode as fast as they leave at the cathode.
The concentration of copper(II) ions does not increase.
No new coloured ion is formed.

explanation:
At the copper anode, Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; at the cathode, Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. The concentration of copper(II) ions stays constant, so the colour does not change.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: What happens to a copper anode?

stem: A **dilute** solution of sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is the main product at the anode?

options.rationale: In a dilute chloride solution, hydroxide ions are discharged rather than the few chloride ions.
Chlorine is the main product only when the chloride solution is concentrated.
Hydrogen forms at the cathode.
Sodium is never formed from an aqueous solution, and metals form at the cathode.

explanation:
The concentration of a halide decides the anode product: concentrated chloride gives chlorine, but dilute chloride gives mainly oxygen (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻).

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Does the concentration of chloride ions matter?

stem: Aqueous silver nitrate is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What forms at the cathode?

options.rationale: Hydrogen forms only when the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
Oxygen forms at the anode.
Nitrate ions are not discharged, and anions go to the anode anyway.
Silver is less reactive than hydrogen, so silver ions are discharged.

explanation:
Cathode: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, because silver is below hydrogen in the reactivity series. At the anode nitrate ions are not discharged, so oxygen forms, and the solution becomes nitric acid.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Is silver more or less reactive than hydrogen?

stem: Each solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Match each solution to its products.
explanation:
Cathode: hydrogen for potassium (and from the acid); copper and silver metal because they are less reactive than hydrogen. Anode: the halogen from a concentrated halide (bromine, chlorine), and oxygen from sulfate or nitrate solutions. Potassium is never formed from an aqueous solution.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Decide the cathode product from reactivity, and the anode product from the anion.

stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with graphite electrodes for 30 minutes. Select **all** the correct statements.

options.rationale: Copper is deposited on it.

options.content: Bubbles of gas form at the anode.
options.rationale: Oxygen is given off.

options.content: The blue colour of the solution becomes darker.
options.rationale: It becomes paler as copper(II) ions are removed.
H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions are left behind: sulfuric acid forms.
Copper, not hydrogen, is discharged.
Graphite is inert, so the anode does not dissolve.

explanation:
Copper is deposited on the cathode (it gains mass), oxygen bubbles off at the anode, the blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic as sulfuric acid is left. The graphite anode is unchanged.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Graphite does not react; which ions are removed from the solution?

stem: A student electrolyses concentrated aqueous sodium chloride in a U-tube fitted with two graphite electrodes. A few drops of universal indicator are added to the solution near each electrode.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What colour does the indicator turn near the cathode as the electrolysis continues?

options.rationale: Red would show an acid.
Green shows a neutral solution; the solution near the cathode becomes alkaline.
Hydrogen ions are removed, so hydroxide ions accumulate and the pH rises.
Hydroxide ions build up near the cathode, so the solution there becomes alkaline.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at the cathode.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the gas formed at the anode.

rejected.feedback: With a concentrated chloride solution, chlorine forms.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe a test for this gas and its result.

points.description: Damp (blue) litmus paper turns red and is then bleached white

parts.explanation: Hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas: it turns red and then white (it is bleached).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why hydrogen, and not sodium, is formed at the cathode.

points.description: Both Na⁺ and H⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode
Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions are discharged (gain electrons) and sodium ions stay in solution

parts.explanation: Sodium ions and hydrogen ions (from the water) are both attracted to the cathode. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen ions gain electrons more readily: hydrogen is discharged and the sodium ions remain in solution.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: The volume of chlorine collected is a little less than the volume of hydrogen. Why?

options.content: Chlorine molecules are larger, so they take up less space.
options.rationale: Equal numbers of gas molecules occupy equal volumes, whatever their size.

options.content: Some chlorine dissolves in the solution.
options.rationale: Chlorine is quite soluble in water, so not all of it is collected at first.

options.content: Fewer electrons are needed to make chlorine.
options.rationale: Two electrons are involved for each H₂ and each Cl₂, so equal amounts form.

options.content: Chlorine reacts with the hydrogen in the U-tube.
options.rationale: The gases are produced at separate electrodes and do not mix.

explanation:
Cathode: hydrogen forms because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen; hydroxide ions accumulate, so the indicator turns blue or purple. Anode: chlorine forms from the concentrated chloride ions; it bleaches damp litmus. In theory the volumes of H₂ and Cl₂ are equal, but chlorine is quite soluble in water.

*Syllabus note: the half-equation in (b) is Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Which two ions are left in the solution?

stem:
Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed using two **copper** electrodes. Both electrodes are weighed before and after the electrolysis.

| Electrode | Mass before / g | Mass after / g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cathode | 25.40 | 25.88 |
| anode | 24.90 | 24.42 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of copper deposited on the cathode.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of copper deposited. (Ar: Cu = 64)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount, in moles, of electrons that passed through the circuit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the loss in mass of the anode is equal to the gain in mass of the cathode.

points.description: At the anode copper atoms lose electrons and go into solution as Cu²⁺ (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻)
The same number of electrons is gained at the cathode, so the same amount of copper is deposited (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu)

parts.explanation: Each copper atom that dissolves from the anode releases two electrons (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻). The same electrons deposit one copper atom at the cathode for every two electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). So the mass of copper that leaves the anode equals the mass deposited on the cathode.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The experiment is repeated with **graphite** electrodes and the same current for the same time. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The cathode gains 0.48 g, and the anode loses 0.48 g.
options.rationale: A graphite anode is inert: it does not dissolve.

options.content: Hydrogen forms at the cathode, and oxygen at the anode.
options.rationale: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper is still deposited.

options.content: Nothing happens, because graphite does not conduct.
options.rationale: Graphite conducts well and is used as an inert electrode.

options.content: The cathode gains 0.48 g, and oxygen is given off at the anode.
options.rationale: The same electrons deposit the same copper; sulfate is not discharged, so oxygen forms at the inert anode.

explanation:
Mass of copper deposited = 25.88 − 25.40 = 0.48 g = 0.48 ÷ 64 = 0.0075 mol. Two electrons are needed per copper atom, so 0.015 mol of electrons passed. With copper electrodes, the anode dissolves as fast as copper is deposited; with graphite electrodes the same copper is deposited but oxygen is given off at the anode instead.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: Two electrons are needed for each copper ion discharged.

stem: Complete the sentence about the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride with inert electrodes.

payload.template: {{blank:cathode}} forms at the cathode, {{blank:anode}} forms at the anode and the solution left becomes {{blank:left}}.

explanation: Brine gives hydrogen at the cathode (sodium is more reactive than hydrogen), chlorine at the anode (chloride ions are concentrated) and sodium hydroxide solution.

stem: Concentrated and dilute aqueous sodium chloride are each electrolysed with inert electrodes. Explain why a different gas forms at the anode in each case, and describe how you could show which gas is which. [5]

points.description: Both solutions contain chloride ions and hydroxide ions (from water), which are attracted to the anode
Concentrated solution: chloride ions are discharged, giving chlorine (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻)
Dilute solution: there are too few chloride ions, so hydroxide ions are discharged, giving oxygen (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻)
Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper (turns red, then white)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Both solutions contain chloride ions from the salt and hydroxide ions from the water, and both kinds of anion are attracted to the anode. In the concentrated solution there are many chloride ions, so they are discharged and chlorine is produced: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. In the dilute solution there are too few chloride ions, so hydroxide ions are discharged instead and oxygen is produced: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. To tell the gases apart: chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper (it turns red and then white), whereas oxygen relights a glowing splint.

explanation:
For halide solutions, concentration decides the anode product: concentrated gives the halogen, dilute gives oxygen.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
hints: List the anions that are attracted to the anode.

stem: Which ions are present in dilute sulfuric acid?

options.content: H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions only, and nothing else
options.rationale: This forgets the ions from water; the OH⁻ ions are discharged at the anode.

options.content: H⁺ and SO₄²⁻, with a few OH⁻ ions from the water
options.rationale: Water is very slightly ionised, so a few OH⁻ ions are always present.

options.content: H₂, O₂ and S, which form at the electrodes
options.rationale: These are molecules and atoms, not ions.

options.content: Na⁺ and Cl⁻, as in salt solution
options.rationale: These are the ions in sodium chloride solution.

explanation: The acid supplies H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions, and the water itself supplies a few H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. During electrolysis the hydroxide ions are discharged at the anode, giving oxygen.

stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed. $120\ \text{cm}^3$ of hydrogen, measured at r.t.p., is collected at the cathode. The cathode reaction can be written $\ce{2H2O + 2e- -> H2 + 2OH-}$. Calculate the amount, in moles, of sodium hydroxide formed in the solution. (One mole of gas occupies $24\ \text{dm}^3$ at r.t.p.)
explanation:
$n(\ce{H2}) = 0.120 \div 24 = 0.00500$ mol. Each $\ce{H2}$ comes with two $\ce{OH-}$ ions, and each $\ce{OH-}$ pairs with an $\ce{Na+}$ ion left in solution, so $n(\ce{NaOH}) = 2 \times 0.00500 = 0.0100$ mol.

*Syllabus note: Cambridge IGCSE Supplement (Extended) content.*
workedSolution:
1. Convert the volume: $120\ \text{cm}^3 = 0.120\ \text{dm}^3$.
2. $n(\ce{H2}) = 0.120 \div 24 = 0.00500$ mol.
3. Ratio $\ce{H2} : \ce{OH-} = 1 : 2$, so $n(\ce{NaOH}) = 0.0100$ mol.
hints: Convert cm³ to dm³ before dividing by 24.
Use the ratio of H₂ to OH⁻ in the half-equation.
